newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia has "political will" for NATO deal-ministry.
newsitem.headline: Russia has "political will" for NATO deal-ministry.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, setting a firm date to sign a deal with the NATO alliance, has shown Russia's political will to cooperate, but a deputy foreign minister said on Friday that the West could yet thwart the deal.
Yeltsin, who flew back to Russia on Friday after talks in Germany with Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said on Thursday he expected to sign a deal with the Western alliance on May 27 in Paris.

"The announcement by Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin is the most authoritative...confirmation of Russia's political will to have a document taking Russia's interests into account," Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Avdeyev told a news conference after a meeting with Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama.
He said the agreement would be signed "unless negotiators on the other side thwart this".
"He has even specified a date to demonstrate Russia's desire and political will," Avdeyev added.

Moscow is seeking a special charter outlining its relationship with NATO, which is expected to ignore strong Russian opposition and invite Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic to join at its next summit in July.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, whose party dominates Russia's State Duma lower house of parliament, told Interfax news agency that Yeltsin had "given up everything he possibly could".
"Now only national security is left, and he has decided to make a deal even on that," Zyuganov said.

"Apparently, NATO made an ultimatum to the Russian president, and none of his friends -- Bill (Clinton), Kohl -- took Russia's interest into account," he added, calling Yeltsin's announcement an "historic mistake."
But Alexander Shokhin, the first deputy chairman of the Duma, told Interfax that Yeltsin's readiness to sign a deal on May 27 was an attempt to force NATO concessions.

"His declaration is a means to apply pressure on NATO's partners," Shokhin, a member of the government party, told Interfax. "Yeltsin apparently wants to advance that 20 percent of questions which are still undecided."

By setting a fixed date, Yeltsin can appear anxious to cooperate with NATO, although he has often expressed his opposition to the expansion plans. If no agreement is reached by then it may be the West that appears uncooperative.
The United States has already reacted coolly to Yeltsin's announcement that a deal would be signed next month.
U.S. officials said a NATO-Russia agreement was anything but concluded and expressed puzzlement that Russian leaders had acted as if a signing ceremony was definite.
"The Russians are, for some reason I don't entirely understand, talking about this as if it were agreed," a senior U.S. official told Reuters.

But the chairman of the Bonn parliament's foreign affairs committee, Karlheinz Hornhues, said Yeltsin's comments showed that Russia no longer saw NATO's plans as a challenge and demonstrated that Yeltsin was committed to finding a solution in time.
"When you set a deadline, it applies to yourself as well as to your partner. So I think this announcement that they'll make it by then gives reason for optimism," he told German radio.
